item.text: {"text":"Evidence supports testing reduced influence for extremely hard negatives rather than assuming monotonically increasing weights. [Hard-BPR (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) directly modifies BPR to mitigate false negatives under dynamic hard sampling; its findings concern collaborative filtering, not proof of gains for masked BERT4Rec. [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) finds that introducing hard negatives too early can underperform uniform sampling and proposes uniform warm-start followed by curriculum-controlled sampling. Conversely, [NARec (2025)](https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1049/aie2.70004) reports benefits from hard negatives in sequential contrastive learning. Together these suggest controlling hardness and timing, rather than universally suppressing hard samples.\n\nFor this benchmark, a feasible experimental hypothesis is a detached, bounded weight on each sampled-negative loss: compare uniform weighting, capped increasing hardness weights, and weights that decline for extreme negative-over-positive margins. Keep masked-target BERT4Rec and one trained network per category. Normalize weights to a fixed sum within each target’s negative set to isolate relative allocation; separately vary the negative-loss coefficient to test total pressure. Fixed weight sums do not guarantee equal parameter-gradient norms, so measure positive/negative gradient norms and clipping frequency. Compare immediate weighting with uniform warm-start while holding candidates, seeds and training budget fixed. These are proposed controls, not established results from the cited papers. Electronics’ reported 11.89% outranking rate indicates ranking conflicts, not a measured false-negative rate; neither margins nor that rate establish relevance. Select using the pinned macro validation HR@10."}
